title: Capacity for Grade 1: Full, Empty and Holds More (with a Free Quiz)
meta_title: Capacity for Grade 1: Full and Empty for Kids
meta_desc: Teach capacity to Grade 1 the way children learn it: full, empty, half-full and holds more by pouring, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Before a Grade 1 child ever hears the word litre, they learn capacity with a jug of water and two cups. Here is how to teach full, empty and holds more by pouring — and the shape trick that fools every six-year-old.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a six-year-old a full water bottle and an empty tea cup and ask which one holds more. Most will point at the bottle straight away — it is bigger, after all. Then pour the bottle into a row of cups and watch their face when it fills five of them. That pouring moment, not any worksheet, is where capacity for Grade 1 actually begins. Capacity just means how much a container holds when it is filled up, and a child grasps it long before they can say the word ‘litre’.

The mistake I see parents make is jumping to litres and millilitres because that is what the exam eventually asks. In Grade 1 that is far too early. A child of six needs to feel capacity in their hands first — fill this, empty that, pour one into another — and only much later attach a number and a unit to it. Get the hands-on stage right and litres become easy in Grade 2. Skip it and the child is just memorising labels.

Start with full, empty and half-full

The first three words to teach are the plain ones: full, empty, and half-full. Use real things from the kitchen — a lota, a water glass, a steel tumbler. Fill a glass to the brim: that is full. Tip it all out: that is empty. Fill it to the middle: half-full. Let the child do the pouring themselves at the sink or over a tray. Wet hands remember better than a printed picture does.

A small thing worth insisting on: ‘half-full’ means the middle, not ‘a bit in the bottom’. Children happily call any small amount half-full. Show them the true halfway line a few times and the idea sharpens quickly.

Holds more, holds less — and why the eye lies

Once full and empty are secure, move to comparing two containers: which one holds more and which holds less. Here is where it gets interesting, and where the real Grade 1 lesson hides.

Take a tall, thin glass and a short, wide bowl. Ask the child which holds more. Nearly every six-year-old picks the tall glass, because tall looks like more. Now fill the tall glass with water and pour it into the wide bowl — and the bowl is barely half covered, or the water overflows, depending on your pair. The shape fooled the eye. This is the single most valuable insight a Grade 1 child can take from the whole topic: you cannot judge capacity by height alone. A tall thin glass and a short wide glass can hold exactly the same amount.

In my experience teaching six-year-olds, this one demonstration does more than a week of worksheets. Do it two or three times with different pairs of containers until the child stops trusting their eyes and starts saying ‘let us pour and check’. That instinct — to test rather than guess — is the whole point.

Compare by pouring

The honest way to settle which container holds more is to pour. There are two easy methods, and both belong in Grade 1:

  • Pour one into the other. Fill container A, tip it into container B. If B overflows, A holds more. If B is not full, B holds more. If it fits exactly, they hold the same.
  • Fill both, then empty into a common cup. Count how many cups each one fills. The one that fills more cups holds more.

The second method quietly introduces the next big idea — measuring with a small unit — so it is worth doing often.

Non-standard units: how many cups fill the jug?

Before litres, children measure with whatever small container is handy. Pick a small cup and ask: how many of these fill the jug? The child pours cup after cup, counting — one, two, three — until the jug is full. The answer might be six cups. Now the jug has a size the child can say: ‘six cups’.

This is called measuring with a non-standard unit, and it is exactly how the NCERT approach builds up to litres. The cup is standing in for a proper unit. Try the same jug with a bigger cup and the count drops — maybe three — which teaches another quiet lesson: a bigger measuring cup gives a smaller number for the same jug. That surprises children, and it is worth letting them discover it by pouring rather than telling them.

Words to use around the house

Capacity is the easiest maths topic to fold into daily life because pouring happens all day. Here are the words and where they turn up:

WordWhat it meansEveryday example
FullFilled to the topA water bottle before school
EmptyNothing insideThe bottle after lunch
Half-fullFilled to the middleA tea cup poured halfway
Holds moreFills up with a larger amountA bucket vs a mug
Holds lessFills up with a smaller amountA spoon vs a lota

A week of five-minute capacity play

You do not need a lesson plan. Five minutes at the sink or in the kitchen beats a printed page. A rhythm that works: one day on full and empty, one day comparing two containers by eye and then by pouring, one day on the tall-thin-versus-short-wide trick, one day counting cups to fill a jug, and one day letting the child predict first and pour to check. That last step — guess, then test — is where the understanding sticks.

One honest caveat: do not rush to litres because an older cousin is doing them. A Grade 1 child who can reliably pour to compare, and who no longer trusts a tall glass on sight, is completely ready for units in Grade 2. Push the numbers too early and you get a child who can recite ‘one litre’ but cannot tell you whether a bucket or a mug holds more.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly what we covered — full and empty, holds more and holds less, half-full, counting cups, and the tall-versus-wide surprise. Every question is worded so your child can answer without a picture. Let them try, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable capacity worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Capacity Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on full and empty, holds more, half-full and pouring to compare. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 capacity: full, empty and holds more

questions.q: A water bottle is filled right to the top. We say it is:
questions.explanation: Filled all the way to the top means the container is full.

questions.q: A cup with nothing inside it is:
questions.explanation: Nothing inside means the cup is empty.
A bucket is the biggest of these, so it holds the most water.
A small tea cup holds the least of these four containers.

questions.q: A glass is filled only up to the middle. We say it is:
questions.explanation: Filled to the middle line means the glass is half-full.

questions.q: It takes 6 small cups to fill a jug. How many cups of water does the jug hold?
questions.explanation: If 6 cups fill it up, the jug holds 6 cups of water.

questions.q: A tall thin glass and a short wide glass hold the same amount. If you pour the full tall glass into the empty wide glass, the wide glass will be:
questions.explanation: Same amount means the water fits exactly, so the wide glass becomes full. Tall does not always mean more.

questions.q: The best way to find out which of two glasses really holds more is to:
options: Pour one into the other and see
questions.explanation: Shape can fool your eyes, so pour one glass into the other to check which truly holds more.

faq.q: What does capacity mean for a Grade 1 child?
faq.a: Capacity is simply how much a container holds when you fill it up. In Grade 1 children learn it through words like full, empty, half-full, holds more and holds less — by pouring water, not by using numbers or litres yet.

faq.q: Should I teach litres in Grade 1?
faq.a: No, keep litres for Grade 2. A six-year-old should first feel capacity by filling, emptying and pouring, and by counting how many cups fill a jug. Litres make sense only after this hands-on stage is solid.

faq.q: Why does my child think a tall glass always holds more?
faq.a: Because tall looks like more to young eyes. The fix is to pour: fill the tall glass into a short wide one and let them see the water fit or overflow. A tall thin glass and a short wide glass can hold exactly the same amount.

faq.q: What household things can we use to practise capacity?
faq.a: Whatever is in the kitchen — a lota, a water bottle, a tea cup, a mug, a bucket, a steel tumbler. Let the child pour between them over a tray or at the sink and compare which holds more and which holds less.
